checklist.title: Is the bloom filter in each Receipt correctly computed from its logs?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify all code paths where Receipt objects are constructed (SG-007: receipt_construction). 2. Locate the logs_bloom() function implementation and verify its correctness against the EIP/specification. 3. For each Receipt construction site, verify that receipt.bloom is computed as logs_bloom(receipt.logs). 4. Attempt to falsify the invariant: (a) Create a transaction that emits logs and verify the resulting receipt bloom filter. (b) Manually compute logs_bloom(receipt.logs) and compare against receipt.bloom. (c) Test edge cases: empty logs array, single log, maximum logs, logs with empty topics, logs with maximum data size. 5. Check for any code paths where bloom could be set independently of logs (race conditions, partial updates). 6. Verify bloom filter is not cached incorrectly when logs are modified. 7. Search for any direct assignments to receipt.bloom that bypass logs_bloom() computation.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0023 | Type: Invariant | This property ensures cryptographic integrity of receipt bloom filters. A violation could allow attackers to craft receipts with inconsistent bloom filters, potentially enabling log filtering bypass attacks. The bloom filter is critical for efficient log searching - if it doesn't match the actual logs, light clients and indexers may miss events or return false positives.

checklist.title: Is the bloom filter bytearray size invariant (256 bytes / 2048 bits) maintained across all operations?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate the bloom filter initialization code in add_to_bloom (SG-001) and verify it allocates exactly 256 bytes. 2. Identify all code paths that create or modify bloom filter arrays. 3. Verify that no operation can resize the bloom array below or above 256 bytes. 4. Attempt to trigger buffer overflow/underflow by submitting transactions with crafted data that could corrupt bloom filter boundaries. 5. Verify bounds checking on all index calculations (bit positions 0-2047 must map to bytes 0-255). 6. Check for off-by-one errors in bloom filter bit manipulation. 7. Test edge cases: empty bloom, fully populated bloom, and boundary bit positions (bits 0, 2047). 8. Verify RLP encoding/decoding preserves exactly 256 bytes. 9. Check consensus validation rejects blooms that are not exactly 256 bytes.
checklist.falsification_approach: Attempt to violate the invariant by: (a) Providing malformed input that causes incorrect bloom array allocation, (b) Triggering integer overflow in size calculations that could result in undersized allocation, (c) Exploiting any resize or reallocation paths that do not enforce the 256-byte constraint, (d) Testing concurrent access scenarios that might corrupt the bloom array size, (e) Sending malformed RLP with bloom of incorrect size.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0024 | Type: Invariant | Formal Specification: forall (bloom): len(bloom) == 256 | A violation could lead to memory corruption, incorrect bloom filter lookups, consensus failures, or denial of service through buffer overflows. The 256-byte (2048-bit) size is critical for the Ethereum bloom filter specification - any deviation could cause nodes to reject valid blocks or accept invalid ones.

checklist.title: Is the bit_to_set value correctly bounded to [0, 2047] by the 0x07FF bitmask in add_to_bloom?

reachability.notes: If the masking is incorrect, bit indices could exceed the 2048-bit bloom filter, causing OOB writes.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate the add_to_bloom function and identify where bit_to_set is computed from the keccak256 hash output. 2. Verify that the 0x07FF (2047 decimal, 11-bit) bitmask is correctly applied using bitwise AND operation. 3. Confirm the mask is applied BEFORE any arithmetic operations that could cause overflow or incorrect indexing. 4. Check for integer type issues: ensure the intermediate value is not sign-extended or truncated before masking (e.g., signed vs unsigned conversion). 5. Verify that Uint.from_be_bytes(hashed[idx:idx+2]) correctly interprets exactly 2 bytes as a big-endian unsigned integer. 6. Test boundary conditions: (a) Maximum 2-byte value 0xFFFF should produce bit_to_set = 0x07FF (2047). (b) Value 0x0800 should produce bit_to_set = 0x0000 (0). (c) Value 0x0000 should produce bit_to_set = 0x0000 (0). 7. Trace all code paths computing bit_to_set to ensure no alternative logic bypasses the masking. 8. Verify the computation at each of the 3 loop iterations (indices 0, 2, 4 into the hash output).

falsification_approach.invariant_statement: forall (hashed, idx): Uint.from_be_bytes(hashed[idx:idx+2]) AND 0x07FF is in [0, 2047]
falsification_approach.mathematical_proof: 0x07FF = 2047 = 2^11 - 1. For any 16-bit unsigned integer x, x AND 0x07FF yields the lower 11 bits, which must be in range [0, 2047]. A violation requires a bug in the masking implementation.
attack_vectors: Type confusion: If the value is treated as signed, sign extension could produce unexpected results
Missing mask: If 0x07FF mask is not applied, full 16-bit values (up to 65535) could be used as indices
Incorrect mask value: If mask is mistyped (e.g., 0x7FF vs 0x07FF) behavior may differ
Order of operations: If arithmetic is done before masking, intermediate overflows could occur
Endianness bug: If bytes are interpreted as little-endian instead of big-endian, different bits would be extracted
test_cases: Feed hash with bytes [0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, ...] and verify all bit_to_set values are 2047
Feed hash with bytes [0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, ...] and verify all bit_to_set values are 0
Feed hash with bytes [0x08, 0x00, ...] at position 0 and verify bit_to_set is 0 (not 2048)
Feed hash with bytes [0x07, 0xFF, ...] at position 0 and verify bit_to_set is 2047

checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0025 | Type: Invariant | Source Invariant ID: bloom-SG-001-INV-002 | Severity Justification: Out-of-range bit indices cause memory corruption (write beyond 256-byte bloom array) or consensus-divergent bloom filters if different implementations handle overflow differently. Bug Bounty PoC: Demonstrate a bloom entry that produces a bit_to_set value outside [0, 2047].

checklist.title: Can byte_index exceed valid array bounds [0, 255] in add_to_bloom?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Verify the mathematical proof: bit_index = 0x07FF - bit_to_set where bit_to_set is masked by 0x07FF, meaning bit_to_set is in [0, 2047]. Therefore bit_index is in [0, 2047]. byte_index = bit_index // 8, so byte_index is in [0, 255]. 2. Review the implementation to confirm bit_to_set is correctly masked with AND 0x07FF before computing bit_index. 3. Check that no integer underflow can occur in the subtraction 0x07FF - bit_to_set (since bit_to_set <= 0x07FF, result is always >= 0). 4. Verify the bloom array is exactly 256 bytes and that byte_index is used directly as an array index without bounds checking. 5. Attempt to craft malicious input (bloom_entry) that could cause bit_to_set to be outside [0, 2047] by examining if the AND 0x07FF mask is correctly applied. 6. Trace the data flow from keccak256 hash output through the index extraction to ensure no truncation or extension errors occur in Uint.from_be_bytes. 7. Verify division by 8 is integer division (floor) and cannot produce fractional results that get rounded incorrectly. 8. Check for any alternative code paths that compute byte_index differently.

falsification_strategy.invariant_statement: forall computation: byte_index = bit_index // 8 where bit_index is in [0, 2047], thus byte_index is in [0, 255]
falsification_strategy.mathematical_proof: bit_index = 0x07FF - bit_to_set. Since bit_to_set is in [0, 2047], bit_index is in [0, 2047]. byte_index = bit_index // 8. max(byte_index) = 2047 // 8 = 255. min(byte_index) = 0 // 8 = 0. Therefore byte_index is in [0, 255].
attack_vectors: Integer underflow in subtraction: If bit_to_set somehow exceeds 0x07FF, subtraction could produce negative values that wrap to large unsigned values
Type coercion bug: If bit_index is stored in a signed type and becomes negative, division behavior changes
Division implementation bug: Non-standard division (e.g., truncation toward negative infinity vs toward zero) could affect results
Chained dependency: byte_index depends on bit_index which depends on bit_to_set - if upstream invariants (PROP-0025) are violated, this invariant fails
Concurrent modification: If bloom array or intermediate values are modified during computation
test_cases: Verify byte_index = 255 when bit_index = 2047 (maximum valid case)
Verify byte_index = 0 when bit_index = 0 (minimum valid case)
Verify byte_index = 0 when bit_index = 7 (boundary of first byte)
Verify byte_index = 1 when bit_index = 8 (start of second byte)
Test division edge case: bit_index = 2040 should yield byte_index = 255

related_invariants: INV-001: bloom bytearray must be exactly 256 bytes
INV-002: bit_to_set is always in range [0, 2047] (11-bit mask 0x07FF)
INV-003: byte_index is always in range [0, 255]
checklist.dependency_chain: PROP-0026 depends on PROP-0025 (bit_to_set bounds) which depends on PROP-0024 (bloom size). If PROP-0025 is violated, PROP-0026 may also be violated.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0026 | Type: Invariant | Source Invariant ID: bloom-SG-001-INV-003 | Severity Justification: If byte_index exceeds 255, the operation bloom[byte_index] causes an out-of-bounds array access on the 256-byte bloom filter. This could result in memory corruption, crashes, or in some implementations, silent data corruption that causes consensus divergence. The mathematical proof appears sound but implementation bugs in the computation chain could violate this invariant.

checklist.title: Falsification Check: Can the add_to_bloom loop iterate a different number of times than exactly 3 (at indices 0, 2, 4)?
checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the loop construct in add_to_bloom that iterates over indices (0, 2, 4). Verify this is a statically defined iteration sequence (e.g., 'for idx in (0, 2, 4)' or equivalent). 2. Verify the loop bounds are hardcoded and cannot be influenced by external input - the indices must be compile-time constants. 3. Check if the iteration sequence is computed at runtime vs statically defined - dynamic computation introduces risk. 4. Attempt to find any code path that could skip an iteration: (a) Early return statements within the loop body. (b) Exception/error handling that exits the loop. (c) Continue statements that skip processing. (d) Conditional guards that bypass bit-setting operations. 5. Attempt to find any code path that could add extra iterations: (a) Loop variable modification within the loop body. (b) Off-by-one errors in loop termination conditions. (c) Recursive calls that re-enter the loop. (d) Nested loops that multiply iteration count. 6. Verify the keccak256 hash output length is always at least 6 bytes to support reading 2-byte pairs at indices 0, 2, and 4. If hash output could be shorter, index 4 read would fail or produce undefined behavior. 7. Test with edge-case bloom_entry inputs to ensure loop behavior remains consistent regardless of input content. 8. Confirm exactly 3 bits are set in the bloom filter per add_to_bloom call by: (a) Creating a zero-initialized bloom filter. (b) Calling add_to_bloom with a test entry. (c) Counting the number of bits set (popcount). (d) Verifying exactly 3 bits changed (accounting for potential bit collisions where same bit is set twice). 9. Verify no conditional compilation, feature flags, or configuration options can alter the iteration count. 10. Check for any wrapper functions or alternate code paths that call the bit-setting logic with different iteration counts.

falsification_strategy.invariant_statement: forall add_to_bloom invocations: loop iterates exactly 3 times at indices (0, 2, 4), setting exactly 3 bits (modulo collisions)
falsification_strategy.mathematical_proof: The loop is defined over a fixed tuple (0, 2, 4) which has cardinality 3. Each iteration reads hashed[idx:idx+2] and sets one bit. Therefore, exactly 3 bits are set per call (unless two iterations target the same bit, which is allowed but does not change the count of set operations).
attack_vectors: Dynamic index computation: If indices are computed rather than hardcoded, input could influence them
Loop unrolling bugs: If loop is manually unrolled, one iteration might be missing or duplicated
Exception during iteration: If an exception occurs after 1 or 2 iterations, fewer bits are set
Short hash output: If keccak256 returns fewer than 6 bytes (should be impossible - keccak256 always returns 32 bytes), index 4 access would fail
Concurrent modification: If bloom filter is modified by another thread during iteration
Integer overflow in index calculation: If indices are computed as idx = i * 2 where i iterates 0, 1, 2, overflow could produce wrong indices
Off-by-one in iteration count: Common bug pattern where loop runs n-1 or n+1 times
test_cases: Call add_to_bloom and verify exactly 3 bit-setting operations occur (instrument or trace the code)
Verify loop indices are exactly (0, 2, 4) - not (0, 1, 2) or (0, 2, 4, 6)
Test with bloom_entry that produces hash with all zeros - verify 3 bits set at positions derived from 0x0000
Test with bloom_entry that produces hash with all 0xFF bytes - verify 3 bits set at positions derived from 0xFFFF masked to 0x07FF
Test with bloom_entry where hash bytes at positions 0-1, 2-3, and 4-5 would compute to the same bit position (collision case) - verify bit is set but loop still runs 3 times
Fuzz test with random bloom_entry values and verify bit count delta is always in {1, 2, 3} (accounting for collisions)

related_invariants: INV-001: bloom bytearray must be exactly 256 bytes
INV-002: bit_to_set is always in range [0, 2047]
INV-003: byte_index is always in range [0, 255]
INV-004: The loop iterates exactly 3 times (indices 0, 2, 4)
checklist.dependency_chain: PROP-0027 is a foundational loop invariant. If violated: (a) Fewer than 3 iterations means some bits are not set, causing false negatives in bloom filter lookups. (b) More than 3 iterations means extra bits are set, degrading bloom filter efficiency and potentially causing consensus divergence if different implementations iterate differently.
checklist.consensus_impact: The Ethereum specification requires exactly 3 bits per bloom entry. If one client sets 2 bits and another sets 3 bits, they will compute different bloom filters for the same logs, causing: (a) Block validation failures. (b) Chain splits between nodes running different implementations. (c) Light client log filtering producing inconsistent results.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0027 | Type: Invariant | Severity: CRITICAL | This is a fundamental correctness property of the Ethereum bloom filter implementation. The 3-bit-per-entry design is specified in the Yellow Paper and EIPs. A violation would be a critical consensus bug. Bug Bounty PoC: Demonstrate a code path where add_to_bloom sets fewer or more than 3 bits, or demonstrate iteration count differs from 3.
